steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the section of an encyclopedia article on application delivery networks that covers the main optimization techniques ADNs use: TCP multiplexing, TCP optimization, and data compression and caching.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- TCP multiplexing
- TCP optimization
- Data compression and caching

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- TCP multiplexing
  - loosely based on connection pooling used by application server platforms for database queries
  - ADC opens a number of connections to servers in its pool, keeps them open
  - client request evaluated, sent to a server over existing connection
  - less overhead from setting up / tearing down TCP connections -> better responsiveness
  - some ADNs also multiplex HTTP and application requests -> run in parallel, better performance
- TCP optimization
  - several RFCs describe mechanisms to improve TCP performance
  - many ADNs implement them for more efficient use of TCP
  - most common: Delayed Acknowledgements; Nagle Algorithm; Selective Acknowledgements; Explicit Congestion Notification ECN; Limited and Fast Retransmits; Adaptive Initial Congestion Windows
- Data compression and caching
  - two types of compression: industry standard HTTP compression, proprietary data reduction algorithms
  - CPU cost of compressing over a LAN can hurt performance; best practice: only over WAN or congested high-speed link
  - HTTP compression: asymmetric, transparent to client, built into web servers and browsers, supported by all commercial ADN products
  - data reduction: proprietary, modifies traffic -> symmetric, needs device to reassemble before client gets it
  - WAN Optimization Controllers (WOC) do this; slowly added to ADN portfolio over past few years as WOCs become more application aware (CIFS, SMB features)

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
### TCP multiplexing

TCP Multiplexing is loosely based on connection pooling techniques that are already established and that application server platforms use to optimize running database queries from inside applications. An ADC opens a number of connections to the servers in its pool and it keeps those connections open. When the ADC gets a request from the client, it evaluates the request and then sends it to a server over a connection that already exists. The effect is that there is less overhead from establishing and tearing down the TCP connection with the server, and this improves how responsive the application is.

Some ADN implementations go a step further with this technique and multiplex HTTP and application requests too. The benefit of this is that requests are run in parallel, and that makes the application perform better.

### TCP optimization

There are a number of Request for Comments (RFCs) that describe mechanisms for making TCP perform better. Many ADN implement these RFCs so that they can deliver applications better by using TCP more efficiently.

The RFCs that are implemented most often are:

Delayed Acknowledgements

Nagle Algorithm

Selective Acknowledgements

Explicit Congestion Notification ECN

Limited and Fast Retransmits

Adaptive Initial Congestion Windows

- Data compression and caching
  - two types of compression: industry standard HTTP compression, proprietary data reduction algorithms
  - CPU cost of compressing over a LAN can hurt performance; best practice: only over WAN or congested high-speed link
  - HTTP compression: asymmetric, transparent to client, built into web servers and browsers, supported by all commercial ADN products
  - data reduction: proprietary, modifies traffic -> symmetric, needs device to reassemble before client gets it
  - WAN Optimization Controllers (WOC) do this; slowly added to ADN portfolio over past few years as WOCs become more application aware (CIFS, SMB features)

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
### TCP multiplexing

TCP Multiplexing is loosely based on connection pooling techniques that are already established and that application server platforms use to optimize running database queries from inside applications. An ADC opens a number of connections to the servers in its pool and it keeps those connections open. When the ADC gets a request from the client, it evaluates the request and then sends it to a server over a connection that already exists. The effect is that there is less overhead from establishing and tearing down the TCP connection with the server, and this improves how responsive the application is.

Some ADN implementations go a step further with this technique and multiplex HTTP and application requests too. The benefit of this is that requests are run in parallel, and that makes the application perform better.

### TCP optimization

There are a number of Request for Comments (RFCs) that describe mechanisms for making TCP perform better. Many ADN implement these RFCs so that they can deliver applications better by using TCP more efficiently.

The RFCs that are implemented most often are:

Delayed Acknowledgements

Nagle Algorithm

Selective Acknowledgements

Explicit Congestion Notification ECN

Limited and Fast Retransmits

Adaptive Initial Congestion Windows

### Data compression and caching

ADNs also optimize application data by using caching and compression techniques. There are two types of compression that ADNs use today. One is industry standard HTTP compression and the other is proprietary data reduction algorithms. Compressing data costs CPU cycles, and when the data is going across a LAN this can make performance worse, so best practice is to use compression only when applications are delivered over a WAN or a congested high-speed data link.

HTTP compression is asymmetric, and it is transparent to the client. Web servers and web browsers have support for HTTP compression built in. Currently all commercial ADN products support HTTP compression.

The second compression technique is done with data reduction algorithms. These algorithms are proprietary and they modify the application traffic, so they are symmetric and they need a device to reassemble the application traffic before the client can receive it. There is a separate class of devices called WAN Optimization Controllers (WOC) that provide this, but over the past few years the technology has slowly been added to the ADN portfolio, as this class of device keeps becoming more application aware and provides extra features for specific applications such as CIFS and SMB.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
### TCP multiplexing

TCP Multiplexing is loosely based on established connection pooling techniques used by application server platforms to optimize the execution of database queries from within applications. An ADC establishes a number of connections to the servers in its pool and keeps those connections open. When the ADC receives a request from the client, the request is evaluated and then directed to a server over an existing connection. This reduces the overhead of establishing and tearing down the TCP connection with the server, which improves the responsiveness of the application.

Some ADN implementations take this technique a step further and also multiplex HTTP and application requests. This has the benefit of executing requests in parallel, which improves the performance of the application.

### TCP optimization

There are a number of Request for Comments (RFCs) which describe mechanisms for improving TCP performance. Many ADN implement these RFCs to provide enhanced delivery of applications through more efficient use of TCP.

The most commonly implemented RFCs are:

Delayed Acknowledgements [1]

Nagle Algorithm[2]

Selective Acknowledgements[3,4]

Explicit Congestion Notification ECN[5,6]

Limited and Fast Retransmits[7,8]

Adaptive Initial Congestion Windows[9]

### Data compression and caching

ADNs also optimize application data through caching and compression techniques. ADNs today use two types of compression: industry standard HTTP compression and proprietary data reduction algorithms. The CPU cost of compressing data that traverses a LAN can decrease performance; best practice is to use compression only when delivering applications over a WAN or a congested high-speed data link.

HTTP compression is asymmetric and transparent to the client. Support for HTTP compression is built into web servers and web browsers, and all commercial ADN products currently support it.

A second compression technique uses data reduction algorithms. Because these algorithms are proprietary and modify the application traffic, they are symmetric and need a device to reassemble the application traffic before the client can receive it. A separate class of devices, WAN Optimization Controllers (WOC), provides this functionality, but the technology has slowly been added to the ADN portfolio over the past few years as this class of device becomes more application aware, providing additional features for specific applications such as CIFS and SMB.

References:
[1] RFC 896: Congestion Control in IP/TCP Internetworks
[2] RFC 1122: Requirements for Internet Hosts -- Communication Layers
[3] RFC 2018: TCP Selective Acknowledgment Options
[4] RFC 2883: An Extension to the Selective Acknowledgement (SACK) Option for TCP
[5] RFC 3168: The Addition of Explicit Congestion Notification to TCP
[6] RFC 2481: A Proposal to add Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN) to IP
[7] RFC 3042: Enhancing TCP's Loss Recovery Using Limited Transmit
[8] RFC 2582: The NewReno Modification to TCP's Fast Recovery Algorithm
[9] RFC 3390: Increasing TCP's Initial Window
